questions.q: Which of the following is a defining characteristic of an entrepreneur?
options: Being resilient
Being a risk-taker
Being legally responsible
Being environmentally proactive
questions.explanation: An entrepreneur is defined by a willingness to take risks — investing time, resources and finance into an uncertain venture in pursuit of a return. Resilience and legal/environmental responsibility may support entrepreneurship but are not its defining feature.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the nature of entrepreneurial activity?
options: It provides financial backing and technical support for a new product.
It provides inspiration and creativity in the development of a new product.
It takes responsibility for the creative and social aspects of a new product.
It assumes the responsibility, vision and economic support for a new product.
questions.explanation: An entrepreneur takes on the responsibility, vision and economic risk of bringing a new product to market. The other options describe only a single aspect — finance, creativity or social responsibility — rather than the full entrepreneurial role.

questions.q: Which of the following best outlines an entrepreneur's activities in influencing the success of an innovation?
options: Examining durability and cultural factors
Analysing market research, legal and ethical issues
Analysing industry standards and production issues
Determining production costs and time management issues
questions.explanation: An entrepreneur takes a calculated risk to bring an innovation to market, so they focus on market research alongside the legal and ethical issues that affect its viability and acceptance. The other options describe production or technical concerns rather than the entrepreneur's market-focused role.

questions.q: How do entrepreneurs support the work of designers and generate value?
options: They create or expand economic activity by promoting new products.
They manage costs and gather research data for production of new products.
They take financial risks to promote social acceptance of innovative products.
They accept responsibility for design refinement and establishment costs of innovative products.
questions.explanation: Entrepreneurs generate value by creating or expanding economic activity, bringing designers' new products to market. The other options describe managerial or risk-bearing tasks that are secondary to the entrepreneur's core role of driving economic activity.

questions.q: Designers obtain patents to protect their designs to ensure
options: effective marketing controls.
the safe production of their designs.
the effective international marketing of their designs.
exclusive rights to license, promote and sell their designs.
questions.explanation: A patent is a form of intellectual property protection that grants the owner exclusive rights to make, use, license and sell an invention. It protects ownership of the design rather than guaranteeing marketing or safe production. In the episode this is the 'patent before you reveal' lesson — the Flow Hive filed a patent through IP Australia before going public.

questions.q: In the episode's GASP-I hook for the agencies that influence innovation, which agency did the Flow Hive's inventors use to protect their design before launching their crowdfunding campaign?
options: Standards Australia, which set the rules their product had to meet
IP Australia's Patents Office, granting exclusive rights to their design
The CSIRO, which funded their research and development
Indiegogo, the crowdfunding platform that raised over twelve million dollars
questions.explanation: The 'P' in GASP-I is the patent and intellectual-property office — IP Australia's Patents Office — which grants an innovator exclusive rights to their design. The Flow Hive filed a patent there before going public, protecting it precisely when it was about to become copyable. Indiegogo (a sponsor/funder agency) raised the capital, but it does not protect the design.

questions.q: From memory: what is entrepreneurial activity, and name three agencies that influence innovation?
keyPoints: Entrepreneurial activity is taking an idea or innovation and turning it into a viable, usually profitable, venture while bearing the risk of doing so.
The risk-bearing is the part students leave out — the entrepreneur invests time and money with no guarantee of success.

Three agencies (any of GASP-I): Government (funding/policy, e.g. CSIRO); Associations and standards bodies (e.g. Standards Australia); Sponsors and funders (investors, crowdfunding); Patent and IP offices (IP Australia); Industry partners (manufacturers).
questions.explanation: If you defined entrepreneurship as turning an idea into a venture WITH the risk, and named three agencies, grade yourself Good or Easy. If you missed the risk-bearing or only listed agencies without the definition, grade it Again or Hard.

questions.q: From memory: what is the key intellectual-property lesson of this episode, and how do the Flow Hive and the powerboard illustrate it?
keyPoints: Lesson: 'patent first, then reveal' — protect intellectual property with a patent before the innovation becomes public and copyable.
Flow Hive: its inventors filed a patent through IP Australia before launching their crowdfunding campaign, guarding against copycats.
Powerboard: the Australian inventor in 1971 failed to patent it and so lost the rights and the rewards to others.
Failing to protect intellectual property is one of the most common ways an innovator loses out — a key legal-ethical issue.
questions.explanation: If you stated the 'patent before you reveal' rule and contrasted the Flow Hive (protected) with the powerboard (unprotected), grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q:
Take-away hot drinks can be provided in a variety of cups, four of which are shown: A — polystyrene foam; B — rippled paper with a plastic lid; C — glass with rubber lid and band; D — double-wall stainless steel with a clear plastic lid.

With reference to ONE of these cups, outline how the designer could protect their intellectual property.
questions.modelAnswer: A designer can protect the intellectual property of their cup design by registering the design through IP Australia. For example, the designer of the glass cup (C) could register the distinctive designs of its rubber lid and band so they cannot be legally copied by competitors.

criteria.descriptor: Sketches in general terms how a designer could protect their intellectual property, with reference to one of the cups shown

questions.explanation: Name the agency (IP Australia) and the protection mechanism (registering the design / a patent), then tie it to a specific feature of one cup — exactly the 'patent and IP office' agency from the episode's GASP-I list.

questions.q: Discuss how entrepreneurial activity can influence the success of a product like a tap turner.
questions.modelAnswer: Entrepreneurial activity can drive a product's success by supplying resources — time, business skills and economic backing — that enable effective market research, manufacturing and promotion. An entrepreneur's networks can promote a tap turner to appropriate niche markets such as senior-citizen organisations, occupational therapists and medical groups, while legal support (trademarks, patents, standards compliance) protects and strengthens the design. Conversely, entrepreneurial activity can also lead to failure if the resources or skills provided result in ineffective manufacturing processes or inappropriate materials that produce a product with minimal function. Overall the entrepreneur's enthusiasm, risk-taking and resource support are vital from the designer's vision through to the final market release.

criteria.descriptor: Identifies issues and provides points for AND/OR against how entrepreneurial activity can influence the success of a product
Provides characteristics and features of entrepreneurial activity that can influence the success of a product
Sketches in general terms and/or indicates the main features of entrepreneurial activity that can influence the success of a product
Recognises AND/OR names an aspect of entrepreneurial activity that may influence the success of a product

questions.explanation: The verb is 'discuss the influence', so don't just define entrepreneurship — show how the entrepreneur and the supporting agencies (patent office, funders, industry) shaped a real product's success, and weigh points for and against. The episode's Flow Hive mapping (self-funding, patent via IP Australia, crowdfunding via Indiegogo, industry manufacturing) is a model of this move.
